Subject: Observability: private forwarder throughput & NAT design

Hi Vanessa,

We are preparing for a compliance review and need specific guidance for exporting logs/traces from the Redwood private deployment you installed in our VPC. A few concrete asks:

- Preferred transport and protocol for SIEM ingestion from a private deployment: syslog over TLS, TCP+TLS, or HTTP/JSON? Is mTLS supported/recommended?
- Should log agents originate connections (push) to our SIEM, or should we open an inbound collector in our DMZ? We prefer the former but need to understand implications for egress and NAT sizing.
- Baseline throughput (events/sec or MB/day) you expect for a medium production tenant and safe burst capacity for incident windows.
- Backpressure/queueing strategy if downstream SIEM is unavailable (disk buffering size, retry intervals).
- How tracing headers are preserved across the stack (we need W3C traceparent or equivalent).

Attached is a rough Novus SIEM requirements doc. Can we book a 30-minute call tomorrow to walk through? This audit is timeboxed to the end of next week.

Thanks David — looping in infra and runtime leads. Summary of our proposed approach and immediate asks below. High level answer: we recommend a push model (agents -> customer SIEM) over TLS with optional mTLS and efficient batching/compression. Details follow.

Proposal (short):
- Agent choice: Vector (preferred) or Fluent Bit as a lighter alternative. Both support TLS and structured JSON/TCP sinks and have solid backpressure handling.
- Transport: TCP+TLS (syslog framing or plain JSON over TCP with newline delim) with mTLS option for customers that require mutual auth. HTTP/JSON + TLS is fine for SIEMs that expect it, but TCP tends to be more efficient for high-throughput telemetry.
- Origination: agents should PUSH egress connections from the VPC to the SIEM endpoint. For private/on-prem installs we recommend a centralized egress proxy or aggregator inside the VPC (sidecar vs central collector tradeoffs below).
- Throughput guidance: for a "medium" production tenant (typical Redwood workload) plan for ~800 events/sec baseline (~20-60 MB/day depending on payload), with burst headroom up to ~5k eps during peak replays/incident windows. These numbers vary with envelope size — provide a sample payload and we will refine.
- NAT sizing: use a HA NAT with autoscaling and tuned conntrack parameters. For AWS customers we recommend a pair of NAT instances (or NAT GW) backed by autoscaling for high connection churn; tune ephemeral port ranges and conntrack timeouts for long-lived TLS connections. For on-prem, use a dedicated egress appliance or clustered load balancer.
- Backpressure: Vector has persistent disk buffering; recommend config with disk buffer sized for 24–72 hours of ingress at expected avg rate and exponential backoff for retries with jitter. If you need guaranteed delivery, set up a local filesystem queue + alerting on backlog thresholds.
- Tracing: We preserve distributed trace headers (W3C traceparent and tracestate) end-to-end. We will add a processing hook to propagate an x-redwood-trace header if the platform generates internal spans. Please confirm Novus wants to receive W3C headers or a custom header.

Action items:
1) Dylan/Connor: produce a Vector sink example for Novus SIEM (TCP/TLS + gzip) and recommended disk buffer settings by EOD. Attachment: rfw-forwarder-ops-checklist.md (draft).
2) Aditya: provide sample telemetry payload sizes from our staging tenant to validate throughput numbers.
3) Vanessa: schedule a 30-minute working call with David for tomorrow 10:00am PT; send meeting invite and Confluence link.

I'll keep this thread as the canonical record.

- Vanessa Ortiz
Head of Solutions, Redwood Inference

On Tue, Aug 3, 2026 at 10:05 AM Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa_ortiz@redwood.ai> wrote:
> Proposal (short):
> - Agent choice: Vector (preferred) or Fluent Bit ...

Quick technical notes and a minimal Vector sink example for the Novus SIEM endpoint. We recommend TCP/TLS with gzip compression and these key params: max_retries, healthchecks, and disk buffer size. Also call out keepalive and connection pooling to avoid massive port churn.

Example (vector.toml snippet):

[sources.app]
type = "file" # replaced by our agent input

[sinks.novus_siem]
type = "tcp"
inputs = ["app"]
address = "siem.novus.internal:6514"
encoding.codec = "json"
compression = "gzip"
healthcheck.enabled = true
retries.max_duration = 180000 # ms
buffer.max_size = 1073741824 # 1GB disk buffer
tls.enabled = true
# mTLS optional fields below (fill certs via customer secrets)
# tls.ca_file = "/etc/ssl/novus/ca.crt"
# tls.cert_file = "/etc/ssl/novus/agent.crt"
# tls.key_file = "/etc/ssl/novus/agent.key"

Key operational notes:
- Buffer sizing: 1GB per aggregator node gives ~12–24 hours of buffer at our medium ingest rate; scale with local disk and expected SLAs.
- Backoff: exponential with cap (e.g., 1s -> 32s) plus jitter works well. Do not block core processing threads during retry; spool to disk.
- NAT/conntrack: set net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max to handle expected concurrent TLS connections. Use longer tcp_keepalive_time for steady streams. For heavy burst scenarios, use connection pooling and reuse sockets rather than opening new TLS sessions each event.
- Tracing header preservation: add a small transform that copies any existing "traceparent" header to the outgoing payload and also sets "x-redwood-trace" when we synthesize traces for internal ops.

I'll attach a short checklist to the Confluence page. Happy to walk through on the call.

— Dylan
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
